_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine seed -- subpoena objection deadlines, federal and
Ohio. Phase 8b, closing the one buildable gap Phase 8 identified and
declined to improvise.
Rule text was read and quoted in Phase 8 (2026-08-23) and is unchanged here.
What is new is the CAP shape the engine gained to express it.
THE SHAPE, and why it is not designated_period. Both rules make the
objection due at the EARLIER of two things: a period the rule computes for
itself, and a date the issuing party wrote into the subpoena.
Fed. R. Civ. P. 45(d)(2)(B)  'The objection must be served before the
earlier of the time specified for compliance
or 14 days after the subpoena is served.'
Ohio Civ.R. 45(C)(3)         'within fourteen days after service of the
subpoena or before the time specified for
compliance if such time is less than
fourteen days after service'
Ohio states the same logic in different words -- fourteen days, unless the
compliance time is sooner. Both were read independently and the identical
day count is a fact about these two rules, not an assumption carried from
one to the other.
DESIGNATED_PERIOD IS A FLOOR ON AN INPUT. THIS IS A CEILING ON AN OUTPUT.
Under Ohio Civ.R. 33(A) the other party picks a DAY COUNT and the rule sets
a minimum under it, so the engine validates their number and counts from it.
Here the other party picks a DATE, the rule computes its own period
independently, and whichever falls first governs. The validator refuses any
rule declaring both, because a rule needing both has not been understood.
THE CAP DATE IS USED EXACTLY AS GIVEN AND IS NOT ROLLED. The computed
fourteen-day period is a period and gets full Rule 6(a) treatment including
rollover. The compliance date is a fixed date written into the subpoena, not
a period this rule computes. Rolling it off a weekend would move the
deadline LATER than the subpoena allows -- the direction that loses the
right -- and would do it by applying a computation rule that does not govern
that date. Stated in the audit trail every time a cap applies.
THE CAP DATE IS REQUIRED, NOT OPTIONAL. Without it there is no way to know
which limb governs, and defaulting to the computed period would silently
produce the LATER of the two whenever the subpoena demanded sooner. The
engine refuses with CAP_DATE_REQUIRED (422 -- the request is well formed and
the rule is loaded, one needed fact is absent) rather than assuming.
THE RESULT REPORTS BOTH LIMBS. When a cap applies, the response carries the
date the computed period WOULD have produced alongside the one that governs.
'Your deadline is earlier than the rule's own period because of what the
subpoena said' is a materially different thing for an attorney to see than a
bare date, and the three states -- applied, tie, not_applied -- are reported
distinctly for the same reason the service-extension states are.
ONE AMBIGUITY DISCLOSED RATHER THAN RESOLVED. Both rules say the objection
is due BEFORE the earlier date, not ON it. Whether an objection served on
the fourteenth day itself is timely is a question about the word 'before'
that the rule text does not settle and this engine does not decide. The
computed date is the earlier of the two limbs as written; a reader who needs
certainty on the boundary day should treat the day before as the safe date.
That caveat is carried in each rule's authority note so it reaches the audit
trail rather than living only here.
NO SERVICE EXTENSION on either rule. Whether Rule 6(d) reaches a non-party
subpoena recipient is a real question -- 6(d) speaks of a party who must act
after being served -- and it was not resolved from primary source. Attaching
an extension on an unresolved reading would push the date LATER, so it is
omitted, which errs earlier. Same disposition as the parked Indiana T.R.
6(G) question, and flagged here rather than silently decided.
STILL NOT COVERED after this file, and the distinction matters: Indiana T.R.
45 ('promptly and in any event at or before the time specified for
compliance') and Mich. Ct. R. 2.506 ('before the designated time for
appearance') set a STANDARD, not a period. No cap, no capability, nothing to
compute. Those refusals are final, not pending.

rules.label: Objections to a subpoena to produce documents — earlier of 14 days or the compliance date

cap.label: The time specified for compliance in the subpoena

authority.quote: The objection must be served before the earlier of the time specified for compliance or 14 days after the subpoena is served.
authority.note: TWO LIMBS, EARLIER GOVERNS. The 14-day period is computed under Rule 6(a) with full rollover; the compliance date is taken from the subpoena exactly as written and is NOT rolled, because it is a date the issuing party fixed rather than a period this rule computes — rolling it would move the deadline later than the subpoena allows. The compliance date is REQUIRED: without it the engine cannot tell which limb governs and would silently produce the later of the two. NOTE THE WORD 'BEFORE': the rule says objections are due before the earlier date, not on it. Whether service on the fourteenth day itself is timely is not settled by the rule text and this engine does not decide it — treat the preceding day as the safe date if the boundary matters. No service extension: whether Rule 6(d) reaches a non-party subpoena recipient was not resolved from primary source, and attaching one on an unresolved reading would push the date later.

rules.label: Written objections to a subpoena to produce documents — earlier of 14 days or the compliance date (Ohio)

cap.label: The time specified for compliance in the subpoena

authority.quote: within fourteen days after service of the subpoena or before the time specified for compliance if such time is less than fourteen days after service
authority.note: The SAME LOGIC as Fed. R. Civ. P. 45(d)(2)(B) stated in different words — fourteen days, unless the compliance time is sooner — and read independently rather than carried over, so the matching day count is a fact about the two rules rather than an assumption. NOT a designated-period rule, unlike every other Ohio discovery rule in this engine: Ohio Civ.R. 33(A), 34(B) and 36(A)(1) let the requesting party choose a DAY COUNT above a floor, while this rule fixes fourteen days itself and lets a compliance DATE cut it short. Computed under ohio_civ_r_6a, whose sub-seven-day exclusion does not fire at fourteen. Same 'before' ambiguity as the federal rule, disclosed and not decided. No service extension: Ohio Civ.R. 6(D) is separately carved out for responses to service of summons, and its reach to a non-party subpoena recipient was not resolved.
